title: Abstraction
description: Abstract classes, abstract methods, and the basics of interfaces, including default and static interface methods.
objectives: Define and use abstract classes and abstract methods
Understand why an abstract class cannot be instantiated
Define and implement a basic interface
Understand default and static interface methods

content.heading: Abstract Classes and Methods
content.body: abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); } declares a class that cannot be instantiated directly (new Shape() is a compile error) — it exists purely to be extended. An abstract method has no body; it's a contract that every concrete (non-abstract) subclass must implement, or the subclass itself must also be declared abstract. An abstract class can still have regular, fully-implemented methods and fields alongside its abstract ones, and can have constructors (called via super() from a subclass, even though the abstract class itself is never directly instantiated) — this is the key difference from an interface, which historically could hold no state at all.

content.heading: Interfaces, Default, and Static Methods
content.body: An interface declares a contract of method signatures that implementing classes must fulfill: interface Payable { double calculatePay(); }; class Employee implements Payable { public double calculatePay() { ... } }. Traditionally, interface methods were implicitly public abstract with no body at all, but since Java 8, interfaces can also include default methods (a method with a concrete body that implementing classes inherit automatically unless they choose to override it) and static methods (utility methods called on the interface itself, like Payable.someHelper()). This narrowed the practical difference between interfaces and abstract classes, though a class can implement multiple interfaces (achieving a form of multiple inheritance of behavior) while it can only extend one class.

content.explanation: Shape mixes an abstract method (area()) with a concrete method (describe()). Freelancer only implements calculatePay() but gets printPay() for free from the interface's default method.

keyPoints: An abstract class can't be instantiated directly and may mix abstract and concrete members
A class implementing an interface must implement every abstract method, or itself be abstract
Default methods (Java 8+) give an interface method a concrete, inheritable body
A class extends one class but can implement multiple interfaces
commonMistakes: Trying to instantiate an abstract class directly with new
Forgetting to implement one of an interface's abstract methods in a concrete class
Assuming interfaces still can't have any method bodies at all (true only before Java 8's default/static methods)
